messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Mariana's Story

Mariana was eighty years old when she finally sought help, though the beating that changed her life had happened nearly a decade before. She had been a social worker for fifty-two years—a career built on her belief that people were fundamentally good, that patience and understanding could reach anyone. That belief had sustained her through the 1980s and 1990s, through decades of case files and crisis calls, through a professional life devoted to helping others find their way out of harm. Then, at seventy-one, she had met Viktor at a church social. He was charming, attentive, a widower who seemed to understand her in ways she had not expected to be understood again. Within four months, he moved into her apartment. Within six, he had pinned her against the kitchen counter one evening—his hands around her throat, his voice a low, furious growl—because she had questioned where he had been that afternoon. The memory came back as fragments: the cold granite pressing into her spine, the sound of the refrigerator humming in the darkness, his face inches from hers, twisted and unrecognizable. She remembered his hand releasing her, remembered sliding down to the floor, remembered the silence that followed. But the sequence of what happened next—how she got to her bedroom, whether she called anyone, how many hours passed before morning—remained scrambled in her mind, arriving in snapshot images that refused to arrange themselves into a coherent timeline.

When Mariana thought about what had happened, she was overwhelmed by a grief so profound it felt like drowning. The memory fragments themselves—the counter, his face, the refrigerator—triggered this cascade of despair, and when grief came, she found herself desperate to escape it. She began to avoid anything that might bring the memory forward: she stopped listening to the radio station she had loved, stopped taking walks at dusk, stopped sitting in her kitchen. She tried, with increasing desperation, to erase the memory altogether, to convince herself that it had not happened or that it had happened differently, to a different woman. She spent hours lying awake at night, thinking obsessively about why Viktor had done this, whether she had provoked it, whether she had somehow deserved it—as though understanding the reason might retroactively undo it. These efforts to make sense of the senseless, to erase what could not be erased, only deepened her conviction that the world was not as she had believed it to be. Her fundamental understanding of human nature—the premise on which she had built her entire career—had been destroyed. People could not be trusted. She was certain of this now in a way that felt like knowledge rather than fear.

This shattered belief system became the lens through which Mariana now saw everything. Because she was convinced that people could not be trusted, she became hypervigilant in ways that exhausted her. She scanned for exits the moment she entered any room, a habit so automatic she was barely aware of it anymore. She could not sleep; her mind would race through scenarios of danger, and when she finally drifted off, nightmares came—violent, formless dreams that woke her gasping. To avoid these nightmares, she began staying awake deliberately, drinking coffee late into the evening, keeping the television on until dawn. Her sleep deprivation only sharpened her vigilance, made her more alert, more watchful, more certain that danger was imminent. And because she felt so contaminated by what had happened—marked by Viktor's violence as though it had stained her permanently—she began to avoid situations where she might encounter men, particularly men she knew. Her brother had called several times; she had not answered. A male colleague from her agency had invited her to lunch; she had declined without explanation. Being alone with any man triggered an immediate cascade of fear and memory: the fragments would return, vivid and unbidden, and with them came the conviction that she could not trust this person, that something terrible might happen.

The triggers multiplied. A door slamming in her apartment building would jolt her into a state of acute alarm, her heart racing as though Viktor were on the other side. The sound of a man's voice in the hallway outside her door would send her into the bedroom, door locked, heart pounding. When her niece came to visit—one of the few family members she still saw—Mariana found herself tense throughout the visit, unable to relax, scanning the room for exits even though she knew, rationally, that her niece posed no threat. But the presence of a male relative triggered the same cascade: the fragmented memories would surface, her certainty that people could not be trusted would intensify, and she would find herself trying desperately to think about something else, to distract herself, to erase the images that would not leave her alone. Each time she engaged in these avoidance strategies—the distraction, the memory suppression, the obsessive thinking about why—she seemed to reinforce the very beliefs she was trying to escape. The more she tried to erase the memory, the more vivid it became. The more she tried to understand why it had happened, the more convinced she became that she had somehow invited it, that the world was fundamentally unsafe, that she was fundamentally damaged. Her sleep deteriorated further. Her hypervigilance intensified. And the cycle tightened around her, day after day, month after month, until she could barely leave her apartment.

It was her supervisor at the agency who finally insisted she seek help. Mariana had taken medical leave six months ago, claiming a back injury, but her supervisor had noticed the tremor in her voice during their last phone call, the way Mariana had become unable to return to work—unable to sit across from clients, unable to be in a room with a man, unable to focus on anyone's pain but her own. At eighty, after a lifetime of helping others, Mariana sat in the waiting room of a trauma clinic, terrified that no one would believe her, that she would be blamed for staying with Viktor, that she would never feel safe again. What she wanted most was to go back to being the woman she had been before—the woman who believed in people, who could walk into a room without scanning for exits, who could sleep through the night. But she was no longer certain that woman existed anymore.
